series: SAE Theory of the State / SAE 国家论
scope: Eight reader essays, complete in Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese and independently written English; not full translations of the technical papers.
method: All eight published papers read in full. Downloaded HTTPS bytes matched the author's local source checkout on 2026-10-25. JSON manuscripts are the rebuildable publication inputs; Traditional Chinese is generated with reviewed contextual corrections.
editorial_boundaries: All three countries and their case records are fictional. The normative argument is not described as current law.
A state is not a subject, without cancelling its legal standing or institutional responsibility. Institutional, official and independently grounded personal responsibility remain distinguishable.
No superior is not immunity. External treaties and arbitration may be effective; domestic implementation cannot depend solely on the challenged office's permission.

Emergency necessity does not suspend questioning or turn state survival into an unlimited end. War-dependent powers expire at the functional end of the defensive necessity; retained functions require a fresh basis and a genuine term.

People affected by an unavoidable state act keep basic protection and a usable, independent, non-retaliatory avenue of questioning without thereby acquiring citizenship or identical positive provision.
Military necessity and the harm to individual persons are separate inquiries. Recording the latter does not alone decide that an act could not have been undertaken.
A common department or appointing authority is a reason to check functional independence, not sufficient proof of capture. Unresolved facts remain unresolved.
Postwar accountability has a non-penal minimum; the papers do not create criminal offences, settle compensation law, or prescribe a unique constitutional design.
